newsitem.title: UK: British Labour employment spokeswoman resigns.
newsitem.headline: British Labour employment spokeswoman resigns.

text.p: A growing row over allegations of sleaze in Britain's ruling Conservative party claimed its first opposition victim on Thursay when Labour's spokeswoman in the House of Lords resigned after defending a lobbyist.
Baroness Muriel Turner of Camden stepped down as the Labour Party spokeswoman on employment in the upper house of parliament after she publicly supported Ian Greer.
The lobbyist has been accused of making payments to former Conservative trade minister Neil Hamilton and 23 other members of parliament or their local offices.

Turner has agreed "it would be inappropriate" for her to remain a spokeswoman in the House of Lords, Lord Ivor Seward Richard, the party's leader in the upper house of parliament, said in a statement.
Labour Party leader Tony Blair, tipped to be the next prime minister and still basking in glory after a rousing speech at his party's annual conference, was quick to limit any potential damage.
"She did the right thing in standing down and doing it straight away," he told reporters at the conference in Blackpool, northern England.

It was the first time the Labour Party had become involved in the scandal which has badly damaged the image of the Conservative Party a week before their annual conference and less than seven months before they must call a general election.
Turner, who is a director of Greer's company, had defended him in a television interview.
"I did firmly believe and still do firmly believe in the innocence of Ian Greer and will continue to support him while I believe that," she told Channel 4 news.
"I am quite certain Ian behaved completely honourably."
In a statement released soon after the interview, Richard said: "There is no suggestion that she has acted improperly in her capacity as a director of his company."
Labour home affairs spokesman Jack Straw insisted that her resignation was a "wholly different order of things" than the allegations against Hamilton.

Hamilton resigned as trade minister in 1994 after he was accused of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
He has admitted he accepted two payments totalling 10,000 pounds ($15,600) from Greer in the late 1980s, but has insisted that the money was paid to him for introducing clients to the lobbyist.
Both he and Greer pulled out of a libel case against the Guardian newspaper, which had published the allegations, hours before the hearing was due to start on Tuesday.
Prime Minister John Major has agreed to cooperate fully with an investigation into the claims which will be conducted by parliament's Commissioner for Standards Sir Gordon Downey.
